**CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (CNN)** — Hospital officials in Corpus Christi, Texas, have launched an investigation after as many as 17 infants in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) received overdoses of the blood-thinning medication heparin—a tragic incident that resulted in one infant's death.

Regarding the status of the remaining 16 infants affected, Dr. Davis reported that 12 remain in stable condition in the NICU, three have been discharged, and one remains in critical and unstable condition—a status unchanged since the infant's initial admission to the unit.

The risks associated with heparin overdoses captured national attention last year following a high-profile case involving the newborn twins of actor Dennis Quaid, who nearly died after receiving a similar overdose at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. 

In November, Quaid's 12-day-old twins, Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace, were receiving intravenous antibiotic therapy for a staph infection. Under standard procedure, nurses were supposed to flush the infants' IV lines with Hep-Lock, a solution containing a small dose of heparin, to maintain line patency. The incident came to light after medical staff in the NICU noticed abnormal bleeding and concerning lab results among several infants. Healthcare teams immediately initiated emergency protocols, including the administration of protamine sulfate—a heparin-reversing agent—and continuous monitoring to counteract the blood thinner's effects. Despite these swift interventions, one infant succumbed to complications stemming from internal hemorrhaging. The remaining 16 affected infants were stabilized and remain under close observation by pediatric specialists.

In the wake of the tragedy, hospital leadership took immediate action to isolate the compromised batch of medication and temporarily halt in-house compounding of high-risk neonatal fluids. The facility has since enacted sweeping corrective protocols, which include implementing mandatory double-check procedures by two licensed pharmacists for all specialized NICU prescriptions, transitioning to pre-packaged, commercially manufactured low-dose solutions where feasible, and conducting comprehensive retrainings on pediatric dosing safety.

This tragic event serves as a stark reminder of the profound vulnerabilities surrounding pediatric pharmacology. Because newborns and premature infants have extremely low body weights and underdeveloped organ systems, the margin for error in medication dosage is virtually nonexistent. What might be a minor calculation or preparation mistake for an adult can prove catastrophic for a neonate. 

State health officials and federal regulatory bodies are currently conducting independent reviews of the facility to ensure the newly implemented safety measures are robust enough to prevent future occurrences, as patient safety advocates continue to call for stricter, industry-wide standards in hospital compounding pharmacies.

**CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (CNN)** — A medical tragedy has unfolded in South Texas as health officials investigate a catastrophic pharmacy error that left 17 tiny infants exposed to massive drug overdoses at a local hospital's neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). 

Officials at Christus Spohn Hospital South in Corpus Christi confirmed that two infants have died, and several others remain in critical condition after accidentally receiving potentially lethal doses of the blood-thinning drug heparin. 

The incident has triggered federal and state investigations, renewed national panic over pediatric medication safety, and brought painful memories of a similar high-profile incident in Los Angeles just months prior.

---

### A Deadly Mix-Up in the NICU

The tragedy began when pharmacy staff at the hospital incorrectly mixed IV catheter flushes used for premature and vulnerable infants in the NICU. 

According to hospital administrators, a concentrated form of heparin—containing 10,000 units per milliliter—was used instead of the standard, highly diluted version containing just 10 units per milliliter. The mistake meant the fragile newborns were administered a dose **1,000 times stronger** than prescribed.

**What is Heparin?**
Heparin is a widely used anticoagulant, commonly referred to as a "blood thinner." In medical settings, it prevents blood clots from forming inside intravenous (IV) lines and catheters. 

In an adult patient, appropriate doses of heparin are vital during surgeries or to treat conditions like deep vein thrombosis. In a neonatal unit, microscopic doses are routinely used to flush IV lines, ensuring the delicate catheters remain clear so that nourishment and lifesaving medications can flow into an infant’s bloodstream.

However, because heparin prevents the body's natural blood-clotting mechanism, an overdose causes the blood to become dangerously thin. In premature infants, whose blood vessels are exceptionally delicate, a high dose can trigger severe internal bleeding, brain hemorrhages, organ failure, and death.

---

### Hospital Officials Express Heartbreak and Promise Transparency

During an emotional press conference, hospital leadership took responsibility for the tragic lapse, detailing the frantic efforts medical staff made once the error was recognized.

"Words cannot express the profound sorrow and devastation we feel for these babies and their families," said Bruce Holstien, Chief Executive Officer of Christus Spohn Health System. "We are deeply committed to understanding precisely how this breakdown occurred within our system, and we are working tirelessly to support the affected families through this agonizing time."

Dr. Richard Davis, Chief Medical Officer at Christus Spohn, explained that as soon as the overdose was discovered, medical teams rushed to administer protamine sulfate—a drug that neutralizes the effects of heparin—to the affected infants.

"Our immediate, absolute focus has been the stabilization and care of these fragile infants," Dr. Davis said. "When the error was identified, our doctors and nurses acted swiftly to reverse the effects of the medication and monitor the babies for signs of internal bleeding. We are continuously evaluating every single child who was exposed."

Dr. Davis noted that while some infants responded well to the reversal treatment, the sheer potency of the overdose proved insurmountable for the hospital's most vulnerable patients.

---

### Echoes of the Dennis Quaid Cedars-Sinai Incident

The horrific event at Christus Spohn Hospital South has drawn immediate and grim comparisons to a high-profile incident at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles.

In November 2007, the newborn twins of actor Dennis Quaid and his wife, Kimberly—Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace—nearly died after receiving identical 1,000-fold overdoses of heparin. In that case, nurses at Cedars-Sinai mistook vials of concentrated heparin (10,000 units/mL) for low-dose flushes (10 units/mL) because the packaging and labels on the two concentrations looked remarkably similar. 

While the Quaid twins ultimately survived after receiving emergency medical interventions, the incident thrust pediatric medication safety into the national spotlight. It prompted widespread calls for the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and pharmaceutical manufacturers to redesign drug labeling, implement distinct color-coding, and mandate stricter double-check protocols in hospital pharmacies.

Dennis Quaid subsequently became a vocal advocate for patient safety, launching foundation efforts to eliminate preventable medical errors.

The fact that a nearly identical mistake occurred at Christus Spohn less than a year after the Cedars-Sinai incident has shocked medical safety experts and raised severe questions about whether systemic vulnerabilities in hospital supply chains and pharmacy protocols are being addressed quickly enough.

---

### Ongoing Investigations and Protocol Changes

In the wake of the tragedy, Christus Spohn Hospital South has suspended the use of pre-mixed heparin flushes prepared in-house, transitioning entirely to commercially prepared, pre-packaged single-dose flushes to prevent human mixing errors.

The Texas Department of State Health Services, alongside federal regulators and the Joint Commission—the independent body that accredits U.S. hospitals—have launched formal inquiries into the hospital’s pharmacy operations, staffing levels, and safety checks.

For the parents waiting anxiously at the bedside of the surviving infants in Corpus Christi, answers cannot come soon enough. 

"We put our trust in the hands of the medical system to protect our most vulnerable children," said one family representative. "To know that a simple mix-up could cost a child their life is a nightmare no parent should ever have to endure."
